Compass & Cub — Expedition Blueprint

Giants &
The Galaxy

Two weeks in California. Sea caves, giant trees, a working ranch, and a sprinkling of Disney magic. The Templetons go west.

July 6 – 20, 2026 Richard · Rachel · Iona (8) ~1,200 Miles
Scroll

The Templeton Expedition

Last time we did this, Iona was a bump. Rachel and I drove the same coast a few months before she was born — now we're back as three, a few years older and infinitely better packed. Coast up to Monterey, a hard turn inland for granite and giants, properly off-grid at a working ranch (where Iona finally rides), home through Anaheim with fireworks. Because of course we do.

Richard handles the planning — it's what he enjoys. Iona is in charge of the pace, armed with her new camera to document the bits he'll miss. Big mornings, lazy afternoons, enough slack in every day to ditch the plan when something better shows up. Nothing here is compulsory — it's just the best version of the day if everything goes to plan.

What to Pack — Climate Matrix
Coast & Marine Layer
12–18°C
Monterey, Pismo, Big Sur. Dense, damp morning fog that often doesn't burn off until lunchtime. The beach doesn't mean warm.
Pack → Fleece mid-layers, windbreakers, denim. Do not pack exclusively for summer.
The Central Valleys
38°C+
Highway 99 crossings, Bakersfield, Fresno. Baking, dry asphalt heat. The car will feel like a furnace when you get back in.
Pack → Breathable linen, loose cotton, sun hats. Constant water. Max sun protection for transition stops.
Granite & High Desert
26°C Day / 7°C Night
Yosemite, Sequoia, Rankin Ranch. Extreme day-to-night temperature swings. T-shirt at noon, needing a thick jumper by 8 PM.
Pack → Layering system. T-shirts + thick fleece/hoodie. Long trousers for evening fire pits. Iona will need a warm hat for stargazing. For ranch riding: jeans, boots with heels, long-sleeve sun shirt, hat with chin strap.

Phase 02

Sun, Surf & Sea Caves

July 7 – 9 · Malibu to Pismo Beach

🐾 Iona's Wildlife Spotter — The Coast Leg Tap a card

Plate 14 · Wildlife of the California Central Coast

Brown Pelican Pelecanus occidentalis Pismo · Big Sur
WhereCruising in single-file lines just above the waves off Pismo Pier and along the Big Sur cliffs.
WhenAll day, but most dramatic at dusk when they plunge-dive head-first for fish — wings folded back, smack into the water.
Spot byA 2-metre wingspan and a huge pouch under the beak. They glide more than they flap.
TallyEasy — you'll see lots. Count to 10 and stop.
Southern Sea Otter Enhydra lutris nereis Pismo kelp · Big Sur coves
WhereThe kelp beds just off Pismo Pier — bring binoculars. Also bobbing in the small coves on the Big Sur drive.
WhenMornings are best when the sea is calmer. Listen for the clink of a rock cracking a shell on their chest.
Spot byA furry brown blob floating on its back, often wrapped in kelp to stop drifting. Sometimes in groups (called a "raft").
TallyTricky from the beach — you've got to look. One spot = a win.
Northern Elephant Seal Mirounga angustirostris Piedras Blancas · Jul 9
WhereThe Piedras Blancas Rookery boardwalk — a pull-off on Highway 1 between Pismo and Big Sur. Free, no booking.
WhenJuly = juveniles and moulting adults flopped on the sand. Look (and listen) for them throwing sand on their backs to stay cool.
Spot byEnormous (males up to 2,300 kg!), wrinkly, and very loud. Males have the trunk-like nose — most July seals are smaller juveniles though.
TallyGuaranteed. The question is how many — hundreds is normal.

🐻 Iona's Explorer Cards Tap to reveal
1 How tall can the cliffs at El Matador Beach get?
Up to 30 metres — that's as tall as a 10-storey building! The sea caves at the bottom were carved out by waves over thousands of years.
2 What were stagecoaches, and why did Cold Spring Tavern exist?
Before cars existed, people travelled in horse-drawn carriages called stagecoaches. Cold Spring Tavern was built in the 1880s as a rest stop where horses could drink water and passengers could eat. It's been serving food for over 140 years!
3 California is the third-biggest US state. How many Englands could you fit inside it?
About three! California is 423,970 km² — England is only 130,279 km². And California has taller mountains, hotter deserts, AND bigger trees than England.
4 Why is the Pacific Coast Highway considered one of the most beautiful roads in the world?
Because for hundreds of miles, the road is carved into cliffs right above the ocean. On one side you've got mountains, on the other a sheer drop to the sea. Some bits took 18 years to build because the terrain was so difficult!

Phase 03

Maritime Magic

July 9 – 11 · Big Sur to Monterey

🐾 Iona's Wildlife Spotter — Monterey Bay Tap a card

Plate 15 · Wildlife of Monterey Bay

Pacific Sea Nettle Chrysaora fuscescens Aquarium · Jul 10
WhereThe Jellies gallery at Monterey Bay Aquarium — backlit blue tanks where they drift in slow motion. The aquarium was the first place in the world to figure out how to breed them.
WhenAll day. Stand close, let your eyes adjust, and watch one for a full minute — they pulse like they're breathing.
Spot byA glowing orange-brown bell the size of a dinner plate, with frilly mouth-arms underneath and tentacles up to 4 metres long trailing behind.
TallyGuaranteed — they're the aquarium's most famous residents.
California Sea Lion Zalophus californianus Wharf · Breakwater
WhereHauled out on the rocks of the Coast Guard breakwater right next to Fisherman's Wharf, and lounging under the wharf itself. You'll hear them long before you see them.
WhenAny time of day — they're permanent residents. Best photos in the morning when the light's on the breakwater.
Spot bySleek tan-brown bodies, tiny visible ear flaps, and a deep "honk-honk-honk" bark. Unlike seals, they can walk on land using their flippers.
TallyEasy — and very loud.
Humpback Whale Megaptera novaeangliae Whale Watch · 13:00
WhereOut on the Blue Ocean Whale Watch from Moss Landing. They feed right above the Monterey Submarine Canyon — as deep as the Grand Canyon — which brings huge fish shoals close to the surface.
WhenLook for a tall misty spout first (the "blow"), then a long dark back arching out of the water. If you're really lucky: a tail fluke, or a full breach.
Spot byBus-sized, mostly black with a knobbly head and very long white flippers. Each whale's tail has a unique pattern — like a fingerprint.
TallyVery likely in July — but the ocean makes no promises.

Morning
Piedras Blancas — Elephant Seals
Pull off Highway 1, walk the boardwalk, and watch hundreds of elephant seals from a few metres away. Free, no booking. In July it's mostly juveniles and moulting adults — which, honestly, is even weirder and more entertaining than the breeding season.
elephantseal.org
Pfeiffer Beach
Purple sand and the Keyhole Arch. The access road (Sycamore Canyon Road) is narrow and easy to miss — it's unmarked, so look for the yellow "Narrow Road" sign. Worth the faffing.
US Forest Service
Lunch
Big Sur River Inn
Order a burger, grab one of the Adirondack chairs, and sit in the actual river. Feet in cold water, redwoods overhead. This is Iona's kind of restaurant.
bigsurriverinn.com
Afternoon
On to Monterey
The rest of Highway 1 north. Check in to the Plaza Hotel and settle in for the evening.
🐻 Iona's Explorer Cards Tap to reveal
1 How big can an elephant seal get?
Males can weigh up to 2,300 kg — that's heavier than a car! They're called elephant seals because the males have a huge nose that looks like an elephant's trunk. They can also dive deeper than 1,500 metres.
2 Why is the sand at Pfeiffer Beach purple?
The purple colour comes from a mineral called manganese garnet that washes down from the cliffs above. The waves grind the mineral into tiny grains and mix it with the regular sand. It's one of only a few purple sand beaches in the world!
3 The Big Sur coastline is famous for its redwood trees. How old can they live?
Coast redwoods can live for over 2,000 years! They're also the tallest trees on Earth — the tallest one ever measured is 116 metres, which is taller than the Statue of Liberty. They survive forest fires because their bark can be 30cm thick.
4 What is a sea otter's favourite trick for eating shellfish?
Sea otters float on their backs and use a rock as a tool — they place the rock on their tummy and smash shellfish against it to crack them open! They're one of the very few animals that use tools. You might spot some in Monterey Bay.
10
Jul

Monterey Bay Aquarium
The Open Sea exhibit is extraordinary — an enormous kelp forest and open ocean tanks that make you forget you're indoors. The touch pools are perfect for Iona. Give it at least 2-3 hours.
montereybayaquarium.org

13:00
Blue Ocean Whale Watch — Moss Landing
Small boat, max 28 passengers. This is a proper cetacean watch, not a party cruise. Humpbacks and blues are both possible in July. Dress in layers — Monterey Bay is cold on the water even in summer. They have a Kid's Corner on board with books and toys.
blueoceanwhalewatch.com
Dinner
Phil's Fish Market, Castroville
In a converted 1869 schoolhouse. The cioppino comes in massive bowls with paper towels instead of napkins. Order the large, share it three ways, get messy.
philsfishmarket.com
🐻 Iona's Explorer Cards — Whale Watch Edition Tap to reveal
1 A blue whale's heart is the size of what?
A small car! It's about the size of a golf buggy and weighs around 180 kg. Their heartbeat is so powerful it can be detected from 3 km away. And a child could crawl through their largest blood vessels.
2 Why is Monterey Bay such a good place to see whales?
There's an enormous underwater canyon just offshore — the Monterey Submarine Canyon. It's as deep as the Grand Canyon! Cold, nutrient-rich water rises up from the depths, creating a feeding ground that attracts whales from hundreds of miles away.
3 How do humpback whales catch fish?
They use a technique called bubble-net feeding — a group of whales swim in a circle below a school of fish, blowing bubbles that form a "net" trapping the fish. Then they all surge upward through the middle with their mouths wide open! It's teamwork.
4 What is the loudest animal on Earth?
The blue whale! Their calls reach 188 decibels — louder than a jet engine. They can communicate with other blue whales up to 1,600 km away. You might not hear them from the boat, but they could be talking to whales near San Francisco!

🐻 Iona's Explorer Cards Tap to reveal
1 The missions in San Juan Bautista were built by Spanish monks. How many did they build along California?
21 missions, each one a day's horse ride apart! They stretch from San Diego to Sonoma and were built between 1769 and 1823. The one we're visiting was founded in 1797 — that's 229 years ago.
2 Yosemite's El Capitan is one of the biggest rock faces on Earth. How tall is it?
About 900 metres of vertical granite — that's more than twice the height of The Shard in London! People climb it with just their hands and feet, and it takes the fastest climbers about 2 hours. Most take 3-5 days and sleep on the rock face.
3 How was Yosemite Valley formed?
Glaciers! Millions of years ago, enormous rivers of ice carved through the granite, scooping out the valley like a giant ice cream scoop. That's why the valley has such a flat floor with sheer cliffs on each side — the glacier ground everything flat.
4 Yosemite Falls is the tallest waterfall in North America. If you stacked Big Bens on top of each other, how many would it take to reach the top?
About 7! Yosemite Falls drops 739 metres in three stages. The water at the top takes about 20 seconds to reach the bottom. In late summer the falls can dry up completely, but in July there should still be plenty of water from snowmelt.
12–13
Jul
Yosemite Valley
Tunnel View · Lower Falls · Mariposa Grove
Tunnel View
The first viewpoint into the Valley. El Capitan left, Bridalveil Fall right, Half Dome dead centre. Get there early for the best light and fewer people. This is the photo you've seen a thousand times — it's even better in person.
Map
Lower Yosemite Fall
Short, misty walk to the base of the falls. Totally manageable for Iona and genuinely spectacular in July when the snowmelt keeps the volume up. You will get damp — lean into it.
Grizzly Giant — Mariposa Grove
An 1,800-year-old sequoia. Take the free shuttle from the Welcome Plaza — the walk to the tree is about 0.8 miles, flat and shaded. This is the one that makes you go quiet.
Yosemite Game Plan

Two full days in the park. Don't try to do everything — Tunnel View, the falls, and Mariposa Grove are the three anchors. Fill the gaps with meadow walks, paddling in the river, and whatever catches Iona's eye. The Valley shuttle is free and runs all day.

🧭 Iona's Explorer Cards Tap to reveal
1. How old is the Grizzly Giant tree?
About 1,800 years old — it was already a big tree when the Romans were still building things! It's 63 metres tall and its trunk is so wide that 6 cars could park around it in a circle.
2. Why is Half Dome called Half Dome?
It looks like someone sliced a giant dome-shaped rock perfectly in half! Glaciers actually sheared away the other side over millions of years. The missing half was ground to dust and washed away.
3. Where does the water in Yosemite Falls come from?
It's snowmelt! Snow falls on the mountains in winter, and when it melts in spring and summer, the water cascades over the cliffs. By late summer the falls can slow to a trickle — we're visiting in July, so they should still be flowing well.
4. What animals live in Yosemite?
Black bears, mountain lions, coyotes, bobcats, mule deer, and over 250 species of birds! The bears aren't actually black — they can be brown, cinnamon, or blonde. If you see one, you stay calm, make yourself look big, and back away slowly.

Morning
Forestiere Underground Gardens

undergroundgardens.com

Arrive Three Rivers
Check in to Blossom Peak Ranch. Quiet, rural, and deliberately slow. The gateway to Sequoia.
🐻 Iona's Explorer Cards Tap to reveal
1 The Underground Gardens were dug by one man. How long did it take him?
About 40 years! Baldassare Forestiere was a Sicilian immigrant who started digging in 1906. He built over 50 underground rooms, passageways, and gardens — all by hand, with no blueprints. He even grew fruit trees underground by cutting skylights in the ceiling.
2 The General Sherman Tree is the largest living thing on Earth by volume. How much does it weigh?
About 1,800 tonnes — that's roughly the same as 10 blue whales or 360 elephants! It's not the tallest or the widest tree, but it has more total wood in it than any other single tree on the planet. It's still growing and adds enough wood each year to make a 60-foot-tall tree.
3 Giant sequoias only grow naturally in one place on Earth. Where?
Right here — the western slopes of California's Sierra Nevada mountains! They grow at between 5,000 and 7,000 feet elevation. People have planted them in other countries (including England!), but they only grow wild in about 73 groves in these mountains.
4 Why don't giant sequoias burn down in forest fires?
Their bark can be up to 60cm thick and contains almost no resin, so it doesn't catch fire easily. But here's the amazing part — sequoias actually NEED fire! Their cones only open and release seeds when heated by fire. So fire helps new baby sequoias grow.
15
Jul
Sequoia National Park
General Sherman · Moro Rock · Tunnel Log
General Sherman Tree
The largest living tree on Earth by volume. The walk down is about 0.8 miles (paved) — the walk back up is the workout. Get there early, the car park fills by mid-morning.
Moro Rock
400 steps carved into a granite dome. The view from the top is ridiculous — the Great Western Divide just goes on forever. Iona can absolutely do this with some encouragement. Hold the railing on the narrow bits.
Tunnel Log
A fallen sequoia with a tunnel carved through it. You drive through it. Iona will want to do this approximately forty-seven times.
Heads Up

The park is at 6,000–7,000 feet. Drink loads of water. The Generals Highway between the groves is winding and slow — don't rush it. Plan for a full day and head back to Three Rivers for the evening.

Morning
Animal Feeding
Early start, cold air, real work. Iona feeds the horses and ranch animals alongside the ranch hands. This is the bit she'll remember when she's thirty.
Late Morning
Horse Riding
The thing Iona has been counting down to. Rankin runs guided trail rides through the basin — beginners on gentle mountain horses, more confident riders go further into the foothills. Lessons start before the heat hits. Bring jeans, boots with heels (or shoes with heels), a long-sleeve shirt for sun protection, and a hat with a chin strap. Helmets are there to borrow if she'd rather.
Communal Dining
All meals are communal — long tables, ranch-cooked food, no menus. You eat what's made, with whoever's there. Just go with it.
Night
Stargazing
Zero light pollution. The Milky Way is visible with the naked eye. Bring a blanket, lie flat in the meadow, and just look up.
Things to Know

No phone service. The ranch has zero cell coverage and no cabin Wi-Fi. Phones are useful only as cameras and torches — which is rather the point. Fishing pond. Stocked with rainbow trout — catch one and the kitchen will cook it for dinner. Iona will absolutely want to. BYOB Patio Party every evening. The ranch doesn't sell alcohol; the office fridge will chill yours. Dinner attire. Change out of the riding kit. No swimsuits or athletic wear at the table — nice jeans are fine.

Ranch Rules

No screens, no schedule, no agenda. The ranch sets the rhythm — meals, animals, riding, swimming in the creek. We surrender to it. This is the deliberate counterweight to everything before and everything after.

🐻 Iona's Explorer Cards — Ranch Edition Tap to reveal
1 How many stars can you see with the naked eye from a place with zero light pollution?
About 4,500! From Manchester you can only see around 200-300 because of all the streetlights and city glow. At Rankin Ranch, you'll see the Milky Way as a bright band across the whole sky — it's our own galaxy seen from the inside, containing about 200 billion stars.
2 How do horses sleep?
Horses can sleep standing up! They have a special locking mechanism in their legs that lets them doze without falling over. But for deep sleep (REM sleep), they do need to lie down — usually for only about 30 minutes a day. They sleep in shifts so one horse always stands guard.
3 The ranch is in a place called Walker Basin. What is a basin?
A basin is a bowl-shaped valley surrounded by mountains or hills. Walker Basin was named after Joseph Walker, a fur trapper and explorer who crossed the Sierra Nevada in 1833. The mountains around the ranch block out all the light from nearby cities — that's why the stargazing is so good!
4 Cowboys and ranchers used to (and still do) brand their cattle. Why?
Before fences, cattle from different ranches roamed the open range together. Each ranch had its own unique brand symbol burned into the hide so everyone knew whose cow was whose. The Rankin family has been ranching this land since 1863 — over 160 years!
5 At the very centre of our galaxy is something called Sagittarius A* — what is it?
A supermassive black hole, with the mass of 4 million Suns squashed into a single point. Its gravity is so strong it holds the whole galaxy together — our Sun and 200 billion other stars all orbit around it. The Sun takes about 230 million years to complete one orbit. When you look toward the constellation Sagittarius, you're looking at the heart of our galaxy, 26,000 light-years away.
Galaxy Night

Look Up

The trip is called Giants & The Galaxy for a reason. The Giants we meet by day — sequoias, granite, the ones that don't move. The Galaxy waits for dark, and Walker Basin is where it shows. No city glow within a hundred miles. Give your eyes twenty minutes to adjust, kill every torch, lie flat in the meadow, and look up.

Milky Way Core

The brightest patch, in Sagittarius. The centre of our galaxy, 26,000 light-years away.

Summer Triangle

Three bright stars high overhead — Vega, Deneb, Altair. The easiest things up there.

Antares

The red star low in the south, at the heart of Scorpius. A red supergiant 700 light-years away.

Sagittarius Teapot

Eight stars forming a teapot shape, its spout pouring stardust toward the galactic core.

Vasquez Rocks
The slanted sandstone formations you've seen in every Star Trek episode, every Western, and probably a Beatles album cover too — tilted at nearly 50 degrees by an ancient earthquake fault, which is why they look so dramatic. Hollywood loves them because they're an hour from LA. Short walk, hot in July, worth half an hour and a few photos.

Arrive Westin Anaheim
Check in. The park's a 15-minute walk away. Walk the route tonight to scope the Downtown Disney entrance — reconnaissance for tomorrow.
🐻 Iona's Explorer Cards — Final Drive Tap to reveal
1 The Tehachapi Loop is one of the most famous bits of railway in the world. What makes it so special?
The trains are so long (sometimes over 1.5 km!) that when they go around the loop, the front of the train passes OVER the back of the train on a bridge above. The loop was built in 1876 to solve the problem of getting trains over the steep mountain pass.
2 Why are there hundreds of old airplanes parked in the desert at Mojave?
The desert air is so dry that metal doesn't rust here like it would somewhere damp. Airlines store retired planes at Mojave for years — some get fixed up and put back in service, some are scrapped for parts, and some just sit. About 1,000 planes have been parked here over the years, including jumbo jets and old 747s. From the perimeter road you can see them lined up like sleeping dinosaurs.
3 Vasquez Rocks have been in hundreds of films and TV shows. Why does Hollywood love them so much?
Two reasons. First, they look impossible — the rocks were pushed up by an ancient earthquake fault and now tilt at about 50 degrees, which makes them more dramatic than any normal rock formation. Second, they're only an hour from Hollywood, so film crews can shoot there and be home for dinner. Almost every classic Star Trek episode where Kirk fights an alien on a strange planet was filmed here. They're named after a bandit called Tiburcio Vásquez who hid in the rocks from the law in 1873.
4 Tomorrow we're going to Disneyland! Here's a warm-up: how long did it take Walt Disney to build the original Disneyland?
Just one year! Walt Disney bought 160 acres of orange groves in Anaheim and construction started in July 1954. Disneyland opened on July 17, 1955 — 71 years before our visit! Opening day was a disaster though: the asphalt was still wet, drinking fountains didn't work, and there were so many counterfeit tickets that 28,000 people turned up instead of 11,000.

17:00
Return for the Evening Session
Re-enter with pre-booked Lightning Lanes. The park transforms at dusk — cooler, lit up, and Iona will have the energy for it after the pool reset. This is the magic window.
Night
Fireworks from the Hotel
Watch the show from the Westin rooftop or pool. No crowds, no standing for an hour in a sea of pushchairs, no exit crush afterwards. Iona gets the spectacle without the sensory overwhelm. Perfect way to close the trip.
The 120-Minute Rule

Lightning Lanes refresh every 120 minutes. Set a silent recurring alarm on a smartwatch to manage the system invisibly — don't let the admin become the experience. Book the next pass immediately when tapping in, or exactly on the 120-minute mark. Don't burn them all in the morning — save at least two for the evening re-entry.

Galaxy's Edge — Queues Worth Doing

The standby queues in heavily themed areas like Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge are part of the experience. If the posted wait is under 40 minutes, join it — the set design, props, and sound design in the queue are extraordinary and Iona will be absorbed. Above 40 minutes, use a Lightning Lane instead.

Slow Morning · Dinner · Night Flight
Morning
No Rush
The flight isn't until 23:15. Late checkout, one last swim, pack slowly. Let the trip breathe its last day.

Last Supper — Sit-Down Dinner
A quiet, proper meal together in Anaheim. Not fast food, not rushed. This is the closing ritual — we mark the end of the trip before heading to the airport.

About 45 mins. Drop the rental car. The late flight is a gift — use it, don't sprint.

Overnight flight. Land 17:35 on the 21st. Connect to BA1374 at 21:35 — home to Manchester by 22:45. Iona asleep in the car by Stockport.
The Logic

The late flight is deliberate. It gives us a full, unhurried final day. Don't fill it — let it empty out.
